```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5)
```

Two chunks start every session. The first is only for this workshop. It points R at the workshop's package library and loads small helper functions that read the prepared data. You would not need it in a project of your own.

```{r workshop-setup}
source("setup/pins.R")
use_workshop_lib()                  # use the packages installed for the workshop
source("R/data.R")                  # load_mammal(), species_status(), site_covariates()
source("R/fit.R")                   # read_fit_summary(): saved results of the model fitted to all mammals
mcp_off <- Sys.getenv("WORKSHOP_NO_MCP") == "1"
```

The second loads the packages, as you would in any analysis of your own.

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(ecoCopula)    # model-based ordination
library(treemapify)   # treemaps drawn with ggplot2
```

## The survey and the questions

In 2023 a team sampled water at 101 river sites across the Gaoligongshan protected area complex in Yunnan and sequenced the eDNA for vertebrates (Ji et al. 2025, *Ecology Letters*). For this workshop, we use the mammals from the survey: 108 species.

Three questions matter to a manager.

- **Where are the species located?** This matters for wild species that we want to protect and for invasive ones we want to control.

- **Why are they there (or not there)?** For example, does human modification of the land keep a species away? Session 2 asks this for the dhole.

- **Where should we protect?** Which sites hold the most conservation value for the cost?

Most eDNA papers stop at summaries of what was detected. This session builds those summaries first, because you will be asked for them. Then it shows why they cannot answer these questions.

## The data

Each site was sampled three times (field samples), and each sample was amplified in six PCR replicates. So each site has 18 PCR results per species.

These are the real survey data, not a simulation. The archive on Zenodo records, for each field sample, how many of its six PCRs were positive for each species. occJSDM wants one row per PCR, so we turned each count into that many 1s followed by 0s. The order of the PCRs within a sample therefore means nothing; only the count does. The prepared copy is in `data-derived/`, and `analysis/build-derived.R` shows how it was made.

occJSDM needs two tables from you, and accepts a third.

- `info`: one row per PCR replicate. `Site` and `Sample` say where the replicate belongs, and the other columns are covariates.
- `OTU`: the detections. It has the same rows as `info` and one column per species, with a 1 where the PCR was positive.
- `traits` (optional): one row per species, with characteristics such as body mass that may explain why species respond differently. This workshop does not use traits.

The species list with taxonomy and Red List status (`species` below) is not a model input. We use it only to summarise and label results, so it stays a separate table.

```{r data}
m <- load_mammal()             # a list holding info and OTU, plus the names of the covariates
species <- species_status()    # one row per species: taxonomy and Red List status
sites <- site_covariates()     # one row per site: its covariates and coordinates
dim(m$OTU)                     # PCR replicates by species
head(m$info[, c("Site", "Sample", "Human_modification_1km", "Filter_vol")])
```

`m$OTU` has one row per PCR replicate (1,818 rows) and one column per species. A 1 means that PCR was positive for that species. In `m$info`, `Human_modification_1km` describes the site (how much people have changed the land within 1 km), and `Filter_vol` describes each field sample (how much water was filtered, which can change how much DNA was caught).

To see the design, look at one site and six species. Each panel is one field sample, and each row in a panel is one PCR replicate.

```{r design, fig.height = 4}
show <- c("Cuon alpinus", "Sus scrofa", "Bos taurus", "Rattus tanezumi", "Nectogale elegans", "Dacnomys millardi")
show_cols <- species$otu_id[match(show, species$species)]

one_site <- tibble(Site = m$info$Site, Sample = m$info$Sample) |>
  bind_cols(setNames(as_tibble(m$OTU[, show_cols]), show)) |>
  filter(Site == "GLG13") |>
  group_by(Sample) |>
  mutate(PCR = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(show), names_to = "species", values_to = "positive")

ggplot(one_site, aes(species, factor(PCR), fill = factor(positive))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ Sample) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`0` = "grey90", `1` = "firebrick"), labels = c("negative", "positive"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "PCR replicate", title = "Site GLG13: three field samples, six PCRs each") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "italic"))
```

The dhole was positive in one PCR of the 18 at this site. Keep that in mind; we come back to it below.

## Summary 1: what was detected, by taxonomic order

```{r composition}
composition <- species |>
  count(order, family, name = "species")

ggplot(composition, aes(area = species, fill = order, subgroup = order)) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white") +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "white", size = 4) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(place = "centre", colour = "white", grow = TRUE, alpha = 0.85) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(title = "Rodents dominate the mammal list")

count(species, order, sort = TRUE)
```

Each box is a taxonomic order, its area set by the number of species detected. The small boxes inside are families.

## Summary 2: an ordination

An ordination puts sites and species on a map where similar ones sit close together. We use `ecoCopula`, a model-based ordination, on site-by-species presence and absence. A species counts as present at a site if any of its 18 PCRs was positive. Species detected at fewer than 5 sites are dropped, because there is too little information to place them.

First, turn the PCR rows into one row per site.

```{r presence}
presence <- rowsum(m$OTU, m$info$Site) > 0    # TRUE if any of a site's 18 PCRs was positive
presence <- presence * 1                       # as 1 and 0: sites in rows, species in columns
keep <- colSums(presence) >= 5                 # species detected at 5 or more sites
y <- as.data.frame(presence[, keep])
c(kept = sum(keep), dropped = sum(!keep))
```

`stackedsdm()` fits a simple model to each species on its own, here with no covariates (`~ 1`). `cord()` then finds two latent variables, hidden axes that best explain which species turn up together at the same sites.

```{r ordination}
set.seed(2026)   # the ordination starts from random values. In this class, we use set.seed() so that all students will get the same output
sdm <- stackedsdm(y, formula_X = ~ 1, data = data.frame(site = rownames(y)), family = "binomial", ncores = 1)
ord <- cord(sdm, nlv = 2)

site_scores <- tibble(Site = rownames(y), LV1 = ord$scores[, 1], LV2 = ord$scores[, 2]) |>
  left_join(sites, by = "Site")
species_scores <- tibble(otu_id = colnames(y), LV1 = ord$loadings[, 1], LV2 = ord$loadings[, 2]) |>
  left_join(species, by = "otu_id")

# Stretch the species arrows to the scale of the sites, so both show on one plot.
k <- 0.9 * max(abs(c(site_scores$LV1, site_scores$LV2))) / max(abs(c(species_scores$LV1, species_scores$LV2)))
```

The biplot draws sites as filled circles and species as arrows, so each can carry its own colour.

```{r biplot-human, fig.height = 6.5}
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = site_scores, aes(LV1, LV2, fill = Human_modification_1km), shape = 21, colour = "white", size = 3) +
  geom_segment(data = species_scores, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = LV1 * k, yend = LV2 * k, colour = order),
               alpha = 0.8, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "cm"))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Latent variable 1", y = "Latent variable 2", fill = "Human\nmodification", colour = "Order",
       title = "Sites coloured by human modification, species arrows by order") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r biplot-region, fig.height = 6.5}
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = site_scores, aes(LV1, LV2, fill = Regional_Division), shape = 21, colour = "white", size = 3) +
  geom_segment(data = species_scores, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = LV1 * k, yend = LV2 * k, colour = local_status),
               alpha = 0.8, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "cm"))) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Latent variable 1", y = "Latent variable 2", fill = "Region", colour = "Status",
       title = "Sites coloured by regional division, species arrows by wild or domestic") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise.** Look at the two biplots. Which sites sit together? Which groups of species point the same way? Write down one thing you could tell a park manager from this figure.

Colours can suggest a pattern that is not there, so check it. How much of the spread of species along each axis is explained by their taxonomic order?

```{r order-check}
share <- function(axis) {
  a <- anova(lm(reformulate("order", axis), data = species_scores))
  c(share_explained = round(a$`Sum Sq`[1] / sum(a$`Sum Sq`), 2), 
    p_value = round(a$`Pr(>F)`[1], 3))
}

rbind(LV1 = share("LV1"), LV2 = share("LV2"))
```

Order explains about a fifth of the spread along the first axis, and the evidence for even that is borderline (p close to 0.05). Along the second axis it explains less, with no real evidence at all. Rodents fan out in many directions. The ordination describes how detections co-occur at these sites. It does not recover the taxonomy, and it still cannot say where a species is.

## The wall: where is the dhole?

The dhole (*Cuon alpinus*) is an Endangered wild dog. Here is where it was detected.

```{r dhole-map}
dhole <- species$otu_id[species$species == "Cuon alpinus"]
dhole_pcr <- tapply(m$OTU[, dhole], m$info$Site, sum)
dhole_sites <- sites |> mutate(positive_pcrs = as.numeric(dhole_pcr[Site]))

ggplot(dhole_sites, aes(Xs.1, Xs.2, colour = positive_pcrs > 0, size = positive_pcrs)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "firebrick", `FALSE` = "grey70"), name = "Any positive PCR") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 7), name = "Positive PCRs (of 18)") +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", title = "Raw dhole detections") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Neither the composition chart nor the ordination can say where the dhole is, or how sure we are. The map above looks like an answer, but is it?

```{r dhole-counts}
table(positive_pcrs = dhole_pcr[dhole_pcr > 0])
```

Of the sites with a detection, many have only one or two positive PCRs out of 18. Is that a dhole in the river, or a stray positive from contamination or the lab? A detection is not the same as a presence.

## Detection is not presence

An occupancy model separates two things the raw data mix together. Whether the species is at the site (occupancy), and whether the survey would detect it if it were there. It also allows for false positives: the false-positive rate below is the chance that a single PCR is positive for a species that is not at the site. Session 2 builds it. Here we only compare the answer with the raw count, using a model already fitted to the mammal data.

```{r naive-vs-model}
fit <- read_fit_summary()
n_sites_detected <- colSums(presence)
naive <- tibble(otu_id = names(n_sites_detected), naive = as.numeric(n_sites_detected) / 101)
model <- fit$occ |>
  group_by(otu_id) |>
  summarise(model = mean(cond_mean), .groups = "drop")
compare <- species |>
  left_join(naive, by = "otu_id") |>
  left_join(model, by = "otu_id") |>
  left_join(fit$params[, c("otu_id", "q_mean")], by = "otu_id")

compare |>
  filter(species %in% c("Sus scrofa", "Bos taurus", "Cuon alpinus")) |>
  transmute(species, status = local_status,
            `share of sites with a detection` = round(naive, 2),
            `model: share of sites occupied` = round(model, 2),
            `false-positive rate` = round(q_mean, 3))
```

```{r naive-model-plot}
ggplot(compare, aes(naive, model, colour = q_mean)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "False-positive\nrate", option = "C") +
  labs(x = "Share of sites with a detection", y = "Model: share of sites occupied",
       title = "The model puts most species at fewer sites than they were detected at") +
  theme_minimal() + coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1))
```

Species above the line gain sites. Species below it lose them. The pig and cattle are detected at almost every site, yet the model puts them at about half. Part of the reason is likely DNA washed into the rivers from farms. But most species fall below the line, including wild ones that no farm explains, such as the water shrew *Nectogale elegans* and the rat *Dacnomys millardi*. The model cannot say why a species has a high false-positive rate, only that its detections are more widespread than its occupancy appears to be. That is a conclusion of the model, not an observation, and Session 3 comes back to it. The dhole is detected at 41 of 101 sites, and the model says it is at far fewer.

## What you take away

- Composition charts and ordinations summarise what was detected. They cannot tell you where a species is, and they cannot separate presence from detection.
- A model of occupancy and detection can say where a species is. Session 2 shows how sure it is.
- Session 2 builds that model for the dhole and maps it. Session 4 turns the answer for all species into a conservation plan.
